strengths: Novel theoretical framework: Theorem 3.2 elegantly decomposes optimal aggregation into PRM and LLM signal components, providing principled justification for weighted voting beyond ad-hoc approaches.

Important insight on negative weights: Demonstrates that optimal functions assign substantially negative weights to low-quality responses, a mechanism absent in standard methods (BoN, majority voting) with clear practical implications.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Tests across 35 LLM-PRM combinations (5 LLMs × 7 PRMs) with consistent improvements, spanning MATH, MATH500, and MMLU-Pro-CoT-Eval datasets.

Significant practical efficiency gains: Achieves equivalent or superior performance using only 21.3%-37.1% of test-time computation compared to baselines, with reasonable calibration cost (break-even at ~127 queries).
Practical and simple solutions: Both non-parametric (KDE) and parametric approaches require only small calibration sets (100 questions) and are easy to implement without model retraining.

Excellent reproducibility and presentation: Detailed experimental setup, full theoretical derivations, use of public models, thoughtful ablations (Figure 3 on negative weights, Section 5.3 analysis), and clear writing.

Reveals model-dependent weighting functions: Empirically shows optimal weights vary significantly across LLM-PRM pairs, providing valuable characterization of aggregation behavior and justifying need for model-specific calibration.
weaknesses: Strong theoretical assumptions with questionable practical validity: Assumption 3.1 (conditional independence of scores and generations) is unrealistic—responses are often correlated, and PRM scores may depend on question difficulty or contextual factors not captured by the theory.

Substantial theory-practice gap: Per-question optimal weighting varies significantly (Figure 4 left); the global weighting approach is acknowledged as fundamentally suboptimal. Authors abandoned meta-model approaches without detailed explanation of why this challenge is intractable.

Theory underperforms in practice: KDE method (theoretically principled) underperforms simpler parametric approaches (Table 1, 4), suggesting the theoretical framework doesn't capture important practical aspects like per-question variation.

Limited evaluation scope: Heavy concentration on mathematical reasoning (MATH datasets). MMLU-Pro-CoT-Eval evaluation is minimal (150 questions/task); domain transferability and applicability to non-math domains remain unclear. No evaluation on other TTS paradigms (tree-of-thoughts, sequential refinement).

Model-dependence not characterized: While showing weights vary across LLM-PRM pairs, lacks principled guidance on what drives these differences. Missing analysis of how LLM capacity, PRM training, or other factors influence optimal weights, limiting generalization to new model combinations.

Modest improvements in some cases: Several results show small gains (e.g., Table 1: Qwen2.5-1.5B with Qwen-PRM at 57.5→57.6, <0.2% improvement). Standard deviations often ≤±0.1 across 3 runs raise questions about statistical significance.

Insufficient ablation on negative weights: Doesn't cleanly isolate how much improvement comes specifically from negative weighting versus other factors. An ablation enforcing non-negative weights would clarify this contribution.

Calibration requirement and limited transfer analysis: Method requires labeled calibration data; transferability to completely new domains not thoroughly tested. Figure 3 shows calibration set size matters, but practical lower bounds unclear.
